definition: A text is 'political' when its dominant concern is the diplomatic, domestic-political, or legitimacy dimension of a crisis rather than the operational conduct of force. Political texts address negotiations and diplomatic exchanges; signaling, credibility, prestige, and deterrence as seen by allies, adversaries, or domestic audiences; congressional and public opinion; the internal politics of foreign states or of the US bureaucracy; international organizations, legal authority, and public justification; and the political objectives or political consequences of action. A text is 'military' when its dominant concern is the operational employment of force: capabilities, deployments, targeting, rules of engagement, logistics, battlefield reporting, and intelligence on enemy forces and military intentions.
clarification: Classify as political (1) when the text: (a) explicitly frames an issue as a political judgment or political objective; (b) weighs options primarily by domestic political costs (Congress, polls, public climate, charges of fabrication) or by effects on negotiations, credibility, morale of allies, or world opinion; (c) analyzes foreign leadership, factions, internal stability, or adversary leaders' motivations; (d) conducts diplomacy - protests, demarches, mediation, UN involvement, alliance consultation, coercive signaling, or proposals for reciprocal de-escalation; or (e) manages the bureaucratic-political process at home (leaks, resignations, interagency conflict). A text may mention military instruments and still be political if those instruments are discussed mainly as signals or bargaining leverage.

negative_clarification: Classify as military (0) when the text's dominant content is: operational planning or execution (strike timing and waves, target selection, force packages); troop, aircraft, or ship deployments and logistics; rules of engagement and hot pursuit; battlefield situation reports and order of battle; intelligence estimates of enemy military capabilities, attack timing, or force structure; technical weapons intelligence; deliveries of military assistance; or strategic guidance framed in operational terms (e.g., seek-and-destroy). Passing references to political rationale (e.g., using B-52s 'for political or diplomatic reasons,' warning an embassy before a mission) do not make a text political if its substance is the military operation itself; likewise, a recommendation to use force is military when it focuses on the action rather than on its diplomatic or domestic-political dimensions.
